reply.title: Why does a sigmoid squash any number into 0 to 1?
reply.story:
When building models that make binary choices, we often need to turn any real-valued score into a probability between zero and one. Linear functions fail here because they grow without bound as inputs get large. We want a smooth, S-shaped curve that maps negative infinity to zero and positive infinity to one.

Mathematicians use the logistic function for this exact mapping. By placing the input inside an exponential denominator, large negative numbers make the denominator huge and send the output to zero. Large positive numbers make the exponential term vanish, leaving the fraction equal to one.

As we adjust the steepness and midpoint parameters, the transition shifts and tilts. The derivative at the midpoint reveals how aggressively the curve compresses inputs, giving us a complete tool for probability scaling.
reply.cardDescription: Explore how the logistic function $y = 1 / (1 + \exp(-k(x - x_0)))$ maps any real number into the interval from zero to one. Adjust the steepness, midpoint, and marker to see the output and slope change.
reply.instructions: Adjust the steepness, midpoint, and marker sliders to observe how the logistic curve squashes inputs.
